content.intro: Variables and Assignment is part of R Syntax and Fundamental Rules. Start with creating variables and connect it to the worked example and expected result.
content.why_it_matters: Assignment binds a name to an object; it does not declare a fixed static type.

content_blocks.title: Why this matters
content_blocks.text: Assignment binds a name to an object; it does not declare a fixed static type. The example is intentionally small so you can predict its result before checking it in a local R session.

content_blocks.title: Work through it
content_blocks.text: Try changing a numeric object to a character value and inspect its type with typeof(). Change one input or condition at a time, compare the observed result with your prediction, and write down one limitation.

content_blocks.title: Common pitfall
content_blocks.text: Do not treat a syntactically plausible example as proof of correctness. For variables and assignment, check the input type, missing/empty cases, output shape, and domain assumptions.

common_mistakes.problem: Using an example without checking its inputs or output shape.
common_mistakes.why: R can coerce types, propagate missing values or simplify results unexpectedly.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect with str(), class(), typeof(), length() or dim() and add a direct check.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a demonstration as proof that every edge case works.
common_mistakes.why: Empty input, missing values, dependencies and version differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Test a normal case and a boundary/failure case in a clean local R session.

common_mistakes.why: The conclusion depends on data provenance, transformations and assumptions.
common_mistakes.fix: Record input source, cleaning choices and known limitations beside the result.
